slides.text: Bhumak or Bhumkal means earthquake or vibration of the land. The tribal movement in Bastar in the year 1910 was large and widespread. That is why it is called the Mahan Bhumkal.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Gundadhur leading thousands of Bastar tribals through Sal forest at dawn. Sal-leaf flags raised high. Ground trembling beneath them. Title: The Earthquake of Bastar. Ink-wash illustration, dark forest greens and fire oranges.

slides.text: In this battle, the entire community of tribals unitedly fought against British rule. In this movement, thousands of tribals of Bastar fought a war for their water, forest, and land. The tribals had waged war against the British rule and their exploiting class.
slides.visualDescription: Thousands of Bastar tribals assembled in a forest clearing — men, women, elders, youth. Traditional weapons raised. Sal-leaf banners. A unified community rising. Dawn light. The scale of Bhumkal made visible. Sweeping panoramic shot.

slides.text: The prominent leaders who participated in this movement were Gundadhur, Kunwar Bahadur Singh, Bala Prasad, Dular Singh, and Nazir. Another literal meaning of Bhumkal is to fight for one's land.
slides.visualDescription: Portraits of the five Bhumkal leaders — Gundadhur at center, Kunwar Bahadur Singh, Bala Prasad, Dular Singh, Nazir arranged around him. Each face carrying the weight of the struggle. Forest background, firelight, honor.

slides.text: While Kanker, Bastar, and other Riyasats were acting as agents of the British, keeping themselves safe and recovering Lagaan with full vigor, on the other hand, the participation of the general public under Gundadhur's leadership turned it into a major uprising.
slides.visualDescription: Split scene: Riyasat princes at a colonial dinner with British officers on one side — comfortable, compliant. On the other side: Gundadhur leading ordinary tribals through the forest. The contrast between collaboration and resistance.

slides.text: The then king of Bastar princely state, Praveen Chand, was assassinated by the British in the land itself. Even today, Bhumkal Day is celebrated on 10 February every year in Bastar, honoring the sacrifice of those who fought.
slides.visualDescription: King Praveen Chand of Bastar — his assassination by the British. Then: present-day Bhumkal Day celebrations on February 10 in Bastar — tribals in traditional dress, flags, cultural programs. History alive. Memory honored.

slides.text: The major form of a mass rebellion against the British Sultanate in Chhattisgarh was the Bastar rebellion in 1910 under the leadership of Gundadhur. Gundadhur is considered the lionheart of Bhumkal.
slides.visualDescription: Gundadhur — the lionheart of Bhumkal — depicted as a commanding figure in the Bastar forest. His posture: power and dignity. The word Lionheart written beneath. A portrait of resistance. The defining hero of Bastar's greatest uprising.

slides.text: Gundadhur fought a long battle to rid the tribals of Bastar from the exploiting class. The people of Bastar are still waiting for Gundadhur. He disappeared — no confirmed death, no grave, no final chapter. The land still listens for him.
slides.visualDescription: Gundadhur walking into the deep Bastar forest — his back to us, disappearing among the trees. The forest swallowing him. No grave, no monument. Present-day Bastar tribals looking into the forest as if waiting. The legend of the vanished hero.

slides.text: Due to this war, the tribals of Bastar had to suffer a lot. Many tribals lost their lives during the fighting. The tribals faced their guns while fighting the British rule with their traditional weapons.
slides.visualDescription: The human cost of Bhumkal — tribal families mourning their dead. Traditional weapons scattered on the forest floor beside British rifles. The asymmetry of the fight made stark. Loss and sacrifice. Somber ink illustration, muted tones.

slides.text: The martyrdom of Lal Lokendra Singh and Rani Sumran Kunwar took place in the same uprising. Lal Lokendra Singh died in Elichpur jail, located north of Amravati in Berar district of Maharashtra. Rani Sumran Kunwar died in Raipur jail.
slides.visualDescription: Two jail cells — Elichpur jail in Berar where Lal Lokendra Singh died, and Raipur jail where Rani Sumran Kunwar died. A warrior and a queen, dying in distant cells, separated by hundreds of miles, united by the same cause.

slides.text: The names that could be known were: Mangtu Mahara, Dhaniram Halba, Dandi Penda, Sitaram Mahara, Kodra, Jagdeo Marar, Gadba, Hari, Balki, Bilav Dhakad, Kondaria, Budhu Manjhi, Hanam, Narasimha, Marka, Bhima, Suku, Jai Singh, Jogi, Korea Manjhi, Jagra Penda.
slides.visualDescription: A roll call of names — each name of a Bhumkal martyr appearing one by one on screen like stars appearing in a night sky. Simple, powerful. No faces, only names. The dignity of naming the forgotten. Forest background, candlelight aesthetic.

slides.text: Among the revolutionaries who were prosecuted and punished were Dinda alias Hind Penda, Donda Penda, Mukund Dev, Murat Singh Bakshi, and Ronda Penda. Seventy-eight were convicted — of whom 26 died in Raipur Jail.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur Jail — colonial-era stone walls, iron bars. 78 Bhumkal fighters imprisoned. 26 dying within those walls. The names of those who died in Raipur Jail: Asu, Kidariya, Korli, Kola, Chandu, Jogi, Tiharu, Donda Ponda... A prison as a grave.

slides.text: All of them were sentenced to life imprisonment and subjected to the torture of the British prison. The names of those martyrs who died in Raipur Jail include: Asu, Kidariya, Korli, Kola, Chandu, Jogi, Tiharu, Dolam, Narasimha, Pandu, Balaya, Badhru, Budhsen, Futaru, Bera, Mangtu, Mundi, Dhasuri.
slides.visualDescription: Inside Raipur Jail — colonial-era cells. Each name carved into the stone wall like a memorial. The camera moves slowly across the names. A prison wall as a monument. Those who died here. Those who should be remembered.

slides.text: In this way, thousands of heroes of the Bastar region sacrificed their lives in the sacrifice of freedom struggle. The third round of the national movement in Chhattisgarh begins in 1920 with the first arrival of Mahatma Gandhi.
slides.visualDescription: A vast field of Sal trees in Bastar — each tree representing a sacrifice, a life given. The forest as a living memorial. Then: the calendar advancing from 1910 to 1920. A new era beginning. The third round. Gandhi approaching from the horizon.

slides.text: Remembering 1857, one remembers Meerut and Mangal Pandey. But before that in 1810, the planned revolution by the tribals of Bastar had paralyzed the British administration and was called 'The Rebellion of Bastar.' It is included in only a few rows of history.
slides.visualDescription: History books open to pages about 1857 — Meerut, Mangal Pandey in large print. Then a footnote: the Bastar rebellion of 1810 in small text, easily missed. The injustice of marginalisation made visual. Big history hiding small truths.

slides.text: Even though the war of the land could not get respect in national history, it is still immortal in folk songs. The hero of Bhumkal is the hero of Gundadhur folklore. The people of Bastar are still waiting for Gundadhur.
slides.visualDescription: A Bastar tribal village at dusk. An elder singing a folk song about Gundadhur to a circle of young people. The song carries the hero's name. Children listening with open eyes. Living history. The folk tradition as archive.

slides.text: Reduce thick black may even block sunlight for a few moments, but when the sun reappears, its intensity shines, becoming brighter and more glowing. There is a belief that as the history of Chhattisgarh will be brought before the general public, it will also be present in the brightest form.
slides.visualDescription: Dark storm clouds over Chhattisgarh forest — then a break in the clouds, sunlight pouring through with intensity. Visual metaphor: suppression cannot hold back truth forever. The sun returning brighter. Hope after darkness.

slides.text: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 in Chhattisgarh. On May 10, 1857, a troop of soldiers, filled with passion for independence, reached Delhi on May 11 revolting from Meerut. They proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader and crowned him again.
slides.visualDescription: May 1857. Delhi. Bahadur Shah Zafar — aged 82 — proclaimed emperor by rebel soldiers. The Red Fort. Slogans of Bahadur Shah Zafar Zindabad erupting. The news spreading like fire across India. Chhattisgarh on the edge of the map, listening.

slides.text: Veer Narayan Singh challenged the British policies even before the Revolt of 1857. When there was a famine in Sonakhan in 1856, he sought help from the moneylender and assured that his grain would be returned when the harvest was done.
slides.visualDescription: Sonakhan village, 1856. Famine. Skeletal cattle, dry fields. Veer Narayan Singh — a zamindar with a conscience — appealing to a moneylender for grain to feed his starving people. The moneylender refusing. The injustice of hoarded plenty.

slides.text: When the moneylender refused to give food grains, he broke the godown and distributed the grains to the public. Veer Narayan Singh, with 500 men, would later escape prison and form an army. A powerful British army was dispatched to crush the Sonakhan army.
slides.visualDescription: Veer Narayan Singh breaking open the moneylender's godown. Grain flowing out to starving villagers. Their hands reaching forward. A revolutionary act of redistribution. Then: the arrest, the escape, the army of 500. One man's conscience becoming a rebellion.

slides.text: On December 10, 1857, Veer Narayan Singh was martyred by the British Raj at the intersection of Raipur in the crime of sedition. The place where Veer Narayan was martyred is currently known as Jaistambh Chowk in Raipur near the Kaiser-e-Hind Darwaza.
slides.visualDescription: Jaistambh Chowk, Raipur, December 10, 1857. Veer Narayan Singh standing at the intersection. British cannons. The public forced to watch. A man being made an example of — and instead becoming a legend. The chowk that carries his sacrifice.

slides.text: All the soldiers of Raipur were ordered to be present to see the execution. This was done so that the people became terrorized and did not dare to raise their heads against the British. But 39 days later, those very soldiers revolted.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur soldiers forced to witness the execution of Veer Narayan Singh. Their faces — some fearful, some barely concealing rage. The intention was terror. The result was resolve. 39 days later, those same soldiers would act. Seeds planted in horror.

slides.text: On January 18, 1858, a group of soldiers revolted against the British. Although this rebellion lasted only 6–7 hours, the 17 soldiers and gunmen who had been arrested had to bear the punishment by giving their lives.
slides.visualDescription: Night of January 18, 1858. The Raipur military cantonment — the Third Regular Regiment. Soldier Hanuman Singh moving through the darkness toward Sergeant Major Sidbell's chamber. 7:30 pm. A 6-hour rebellion that changed nothing — and everything.

slides.text: People of all castes and religions were among the seventeen martyrs of the rebellion led by Hanuman Singh — which is a symbol of the great sense of national interest instilled in the people of this region.
slides.visualDescription: The seventeen martyrs of the Raipur mutiny — their names on a memorial wall: Ghazi Khan, Havaldar Badlu, Hayat, Munim, Shivnarayan, Pannalal, Maatadin, Bukaram, Bilhu, Akbar Hussain, Lalsingh, Bablu, Paranand, Shobharam, Durgaprasad, Nazar Muhammad, Shiva, Devidin. All castes, all faiths.

slides.text: Hanuman Singh, the main accused in the murder of Sergeant Major Sidbell, escaped. The British government had announced a cash reward of Rs 500 for his arrest. Despite the lure of such a huge amount, he could not be arrested. He never came back.
slides.visualDescription: Hanuman Singh disappearing into the night — running from the cantonment, into the darkness of Chhattisgarh. Wanted posters with Rs 500 reward. No arrest. No trace. Another hero swallowed by the forest. The British helpless before a man they cannot find.

slides.text: Surendra Sai, a freedom fighter of 1857, was a zamindar of Sambalpur, Orissa. He was the rightful heir of the princely state of Sambalpur but was denied his throne by the British, who placed a widow queen instead.
slides.visualDescription: Surendra Sai — proud, wronged zamindar — looking at the throne of Sambalpur that should have been his. The British installing a widow queen instead. A man denied his birthright. His rebellion spreading from Sambalpur to Bilaspur to Kalahandi.

slides.text: Surendra Sai troubled the British a lot in the revolt of 1857. He was arrested from his house on 13 January 1862. Sent from Raipur Jail to Nagpur Jail and then to Asirgarh Fort. He died a natural death on 23 May 1884. At last, he went blind.
slides.visualDescription: Surendra Sai in Asirgarh Fort — an old man now, blind, but still upright. The fortress walls around him. Decades of imprisonment. Dying not by execution but by time. His last years: darkness and dignity. People honor him as The Last Martyr of 1857.

slides.text: In the revolution of 1857, the king of Sarangarh supported the British government. The revolutionary named Kamal Singh was tricked and handed over to the British and in 1867, Kamal Singh was hanged — betrayed by a king who chose comfort over country.
slides.visualDescription: Kamal Singh being led to the gallows in Sarangarh, 1867. A king's betrayal made visible — the Sarangarh ruler watching from a palace window. The revolutionary calm before death. The cost of treachery measured in lives. Stark and somber.

slides.text: According to the British source, the freedom struggle of 1857 was crushed — but the fire of freedom never extinguished in this region. As a spark within the pile of ashes, it kept smoldering.
slides.visualDescription: Ashes from a fire — but within them, a single ember glowing red. The ember of resistance. British records declaring the rebellion crushed — but the ember persisting. Visual metaphor of hope beneath suppression. Darkness with a single point of light.

slides.text: It erupts as time passed — sometimes in the Rajnandgaon Riyasat under the leadership of Sevata Thakur, sometimes in Sarguja under the leadership of the Bagud Baniya, sometimes in Kawardha under the leadership of Ganpatlal Chandravanshi, and sometimes in Bastar under the leadership of Gundadhur.
slides.visualDescription: The map of Chhattisgarh — flames erupting at different points across decades. Rajnandgaon, Sarguja, Kawardha, Bastar — each a new fire from the same smoldering ember. The geography of resistance. Restless, relentless, repeated.

slides.text: They all became revolutionary martyrs. In Chhattisgarh, national level movements were in effect led by the freedom fighters of the state — from the revolution of 1857 which continued till the attainment of independence of India.
slides.visualDescription: A long procession of freedom fighters — from 1825 to 1947 — marching across the landscape of Chhattisgarh. Each era's warriors following the last. The continuity of sacrifice. A river of resistance flowing across 120 years of history.

slides.text: There was a substantial revolution against the British Empire. As a result of these revolutions in Chhattisgarh, there were rebellions in many areas against the exploitative governance of the British. The soil was prepared.
slides.visualDescription: The soil of Chhattisgarh — rich, red, watered by sacrifice. Hands pressing into it, planting seeds. A metaphor for how each rebellion prepared the ground for the next. The farmer and the freedom fighter as one. Warm, grounded, resolute.

slides.text: From 1824 to 1910 — from Gaind Singh to Gundadhur — Chhattisgarh produced martyr after martyr. Each one unknown to the wider world. Each one essential to the story of India's freedom.
slides.visualDescription: A timeline running from 1824 to 1910 — portraits of martyrs at each point. Gaind Singh, Veer Narayan Singh, the 17 soldiers, Surendra Sai, Gundadhur. A genealogy of sacrifice. Each face looking forward to the next generation.

slides.text: The people of Bastar are still waiting for Gundadhur. He fought a long battle, then disappeared. No grave, no final chapter. Only the forest, only the folk songs, only the February 10 celebration every year.
slides.visualDescription: Present-day Bastar — February 10, Bhumkal Day. Tribal people in traditional attire gathering at the site of the 1910 uprising. An elder looking toward the forest with an expression of patient waiting. Gundadhur may yet return.

slides.text: The Bhumkal — the earthquake of Bastar — shook the colonial administration to its core. Even though it was suppressed by modern weapons and mass imprisonment, it proved that the spirit of the land could not be contained.
slides.visualDescription: A visual earthquake across the map of Bastar — the colonial administration's records scattering, their ledgers falling. Then stillness. The forest standing after the storm. The spirit of the land proven indestructible. Powerful, quiet aftermath.

slides.text: In Chhattisgarh, the interest in higher education and social reform that followed was also part of this long awakening. Dau Tularam Parganiha became the first graduate, Daulatram Mishra the first barrister — new weapons for a new era of resistance.
slides.visualDescription: A young man receiving his degree — the first graduate of Chhattisgarh. The pen as sword, education as resistance. From bows and arrows to books and courts. The evolution of the freedom struggle. New generation, new tools, same purpose.

slides.text: From tribal rebellion to organised resistance. From arrows to arguments. From forest ambushes to Congress sessions. The third era of the freedom movement in Chhattisgarh was beginning — and it would need a new kind of leader.
slides.visualDescription: The transition from tribal weapons to Congress flags — a visual bridge between eras. Bows and spears transforming into pens and tricolor flags. The forest fighters becoming city organisers. A new chapter of the same struggle being written.

slides.text: The flame of armed revolt dims. A new kind of warrior emerges — one who fights with truth, with discipline, with sacrifice. Next: Episode 4 — The Cannon at Jaistambh.
slides.visualDescription: Jaistambh Chowk, Raipur — the intersection where Veer Narayan Singh was martyred. The cannon still visible. The crowd of 1857 fading into the crowd of 1920. History layered on the same ground. Title card: Episode 4 — The Cannon at Jaistambh.
